biography.name: Caleb Whitlock

background.family: Lives with grandparents; parents remain in contact but do not provide daily care.
background.finances: Grandparents own their home and live on fixed retirement income.
background.cultureLanguages: English; family attends a small church, though Caleb is undecided about participation.
background.school: Small public school with mixed-grade electives.
background.accessOpportunities: Workshop at home; long drives to specialized courses.

timeline.story: In 2014, Caleb helped his grandmother sort donated books and mostly chose the ones with maps. His grandfather showed him how to sand wood scraps, but insisted that sharp tools were for later years.

At six, he moved permanently into his grandparents’ home after several changes in his parents’ housing. In 2017, predictable breakfasts and the same school bus stop became reassuring parts of an otherwise confusing period.

In 2018, Caleb joined a children’s choir and surprised himself by enjoying performance. He also collected beetles in temporary jars, releasing them after drawing their legs and arguing with a cousin about whether insects slept.

During 2020, his grandparents kept strict household routines. Caleb learned to email photographs of homework from a phone and listened to long radio programs while making small wooden boxes with increasingly complicated internal dividers.
At twelve, he grew self-conscious about choir and stopped attending for a term. A teacher invited him to read a character in a class play, and by 2023 he was singing again with two friends.

In 2024, Caleb sold several handmade boxes at a community sale, then decided he disliked fulfilling identical orders. In 2025, he spent more time learning bird calls and helping repaint the church’s stage scenery.

At sixteen in 2026, Caleb is considering a Texas community-college woodworking demonstration and a university natural-history event. He wants more independence, but worries that moving away would leave his grandparents with too many household tasks. He recently borrowed a field guide and found several of his confident bird identifications were mistaken.

avoids: Questions about parental history from acquaintances
ambitions: He imagines keeping ties to a quiet place while having enough independence to travel and make things on his own terms.

biography.selfDescription: I enjoy living somewhere quiet, but I do wonder what I am missing. Making one good box is satisfying; making twenty just because someone will buy them sounds much less interesting to me.
openQuestions: Does his reluctance to leave reflect preference or obligation?
Would selling varied work feel different from repeat orders?

questions.scene: A drawn creature needs to look surprised, then return to what it was doing. Its shapes must change across several images so the change feels like one moving character.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: In your head, picture three versions of a simple face: before, during, and after a surprise. Consider which shapes you would change and which you would keep recognizable.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore making images become moving characters or effects, rather than only looking at finished images? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Enjoying a finished animation does not establish interest in repeatedly making its individual images.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to create drawings or digital models that become moving characters, objects, or visual effects for animation as a regular part of your work?

questions.scene: A short moving scene shows a character notice a rolling ball and step aside. Viewers keep missing the moment when the character notices it, so the timing and movement need revision.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine the same scene with a long pause before the step, then with no pause. Consider which movement or timing you would revise to make the action clear.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore planning a moving scene and repeatedly revising its timing or appearance? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: This imagined scene does not reveal how you would feel about many rounds of small revisions.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to plan animated scenes and revise their movement, timing, or appearance to make the intended action clear as a regular part of your work?

biography.name: Devin Laurent

background.family: Lives with his mother and stepmother; an adult half-sister visits frequently.
background.finances: Low-to-moderate income with dependable rent and essentials.
background.geography: Apartment complex in Baton Rouge, Louisiana; relatives in Beaumont, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English; family preserves some Louisiana Creole recipes and expressions.
background.school: Public high school with a strong culinary elective and limited advanced sciences.
background.accessOpportunities: Community center and relatives can support occasional Texas campus trips.

timeline.story: In 2014, Devin spent time in his grandmother’s kitchen and disliked sticky dough on his hands. He preferred arranging the serving table, counting chairs, and deciding where everyone could sit without blocking the doorway.
At six, he joined a recreation-center chess group. In 2017, he lost many games to an older neighbor but returned because reviewing the game afterward felt like solving a puzzle with another person.

In 2018, Devin began weekend visits to cousins in Beaumont. Their crowded, cheerful house made him curious about different routines, and he started keeping a notebook comparing bus routes and public playgrounds between the cities.

During 2020, he shared a laptop with his mother and learned to plan work around her evening classes. He cooked simple meals despite still disliking some textures, using utensils and gloves when they helped.

At twelve, Devin tried basketball and decided he preferred keeping score to playing. By 2023, he was helping a community-center coach settle scheduling disagreements and discovering that adults sometimes needed the same reminders as children.

In 2024, a culinary elective made him interested in safe food storage and scaling recipes. In 2025, he volunteered for event setup, enjoying the planning while sometimes finding the constant conversation afterward unexpectedly tiring.

At sixteen in 2026, Devin is comparing Louisiana options with Texas programs near family in Beaumont. He likes the idea of college but is equally interested in whether a short credential would give him something tangible to build on.

ambitions: He imagines a dependable home near relatives, a few close friendships, and a daily rhythm with both busy collaboration and quiet hours.

biography.selfDescription: I enjoy making a gathering happen, and I might still leave early once it is happening. I do not have one big plan; I want to try something long enough to know whether I like the everyday parts.
openQuestions: Would event planning remain enjoyable under deadline pressure?
Is Texas appealing because of programs or because cousins are there?

questions.scene: Several departments need reliable help from a small support team. Someone must organize staff responsibilities and the service budget while checking that essential requests are actually completed.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine three requests arriving together: a missing essential supply, a routine record update, and a room booking next month. Consider what you would ask before assigning staff time and funds.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore overseeing support staff and budgets while being accountable for reliable help? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Choosing an order for three requests does not establish interest in ongoing staff supervision and budget responsibility.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to oversee support staff and service budgets while making sure departments receive reliable administrative help?

questions.scene: One dispute process allows only a voluntary agreement; another authorizes a decision. Participants need fair opportunities to be heard and a clear record of what the process actually produced.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine writing the outcome of a fictional disagreement. Consider what you would record differently if both sides agreed versus a designated person made a decision.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore conducting fair proceedings and accurately documenting an agreement or authorized decision? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Knowing these two outcomes differ does not establish readiness to conduct a formal proceeding.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to conduct fair proceedings and clearly document the outcome while respecting whether the process calls for agreement or a decision?

biography.name: Nadia Flores

background.family: Lives with an older sister and sister’s spouse under a stable guardianship arrangement.
background.finances: Limited but predictable household income; Nadia contributes occasional earnings.
background.cultureLanguages: English and Spanish; close relationships across both sides of her family.
background.school: Public high school; transferred after father’s incarceration in 2023.
background.accessOpportunities: School counselor, free recreation programs, and a supportive employer.

timeline.story: In 2014, Nadia spent afternoons making costumes from old scarves with her sister. She preferred directing a scene to appearing in it and became indignant when an adult audience laughed during a supposedly tragic moment.

At six, she joined a library reading challenge and chose books about strange historical accidents. In 2017, she started a folder of facts that sounded invented, enjoying the task of checking whether each one was true.

In 2018, Nadia tried martial arts and liked drills more than sparring. She made friends through the repeated practice and learned that she could ask to slow down without abandoning an activity that otherwise interested her.

During 2020, she shared school space with her father working irregular hours nearby. She developed a habit of studying late because the apartment was quieter, which helped concentration but made early online meetings difficult.

In 2023, her father’s incarceration led to a move into her sister’s household. School transfer and uncertainty were difficult; a counselor helped with routines, and Nadia kept contact with her father within the family’s agreed boundaries.

In 2024, Nadia resumed martial arts at a new center and began weekend work at a bakery counter. In 2025, she researched the history of a neighborhood building for an assignment and interviewed residents with differing memories.

At sixteen in 2026, Nadia is comparing Texas community-college offerings and a university public-history event. She wants opportunities beyond her current neighborhood while keeping the stable relationships she has worked hard to rebuild in ordinary daily routines.

ambitions: She imagines a secure household with space for friends and enough flexibility to stay connected to family.

biography.selfDescription: I would like people to know me for what I am interested in before they know the complicated family part. I enjoy checking stories, including the ones adults tell confidently, and I still like something as straightforward as practicing a kick.
openQuestions: Does research appeal beyond personally meaningful local subjects?
How much distance would feel like opportunity rather than another disruption?

questions.scene: A person gives a spoken or signed message to someone who uses another language. The message needs to cross languages accurately, without adding advice or leaving out an awkward detail.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine a fictional message: “I can attend Tuesday only if the time changes.” Restate it in simpler words without changing its condition; no second-language knowledge is needed.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore learning to convey spoken or signed messages accurately between languages? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Rephrasing in one language does not test language proficiency or the demands of interpreting in real time.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to convey someone’s spoken or signed message accurately from one language into another?

questions.scene: Someone says “That was interesting” with a doubtful tone. A word-for-word version in another language might sound enthusiastic, so context and intended tone need attention.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine that phrase said with delight and then with doubt. Consider what context you would ask about before choosing wording that preserves the intended message.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore working out meaning and tone across languages, including ambiguous messages? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Noticing tone here does not establish the language knowledge or sustained concentration the full activity requires.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to work out meaning and context across languages so the translated message preserves the speaker’s intent and tone?

biography.name: Zara Hassan

background.family: Lives with her mother, father, and younger brother; extended family is nearby.
background.finances: Moderate income; one parent recently returned to part-time work.
background.cultureLanguages: English and Arabic; Muslim household with room for individual preferences.
background.school: Public high school; treated for major depressive disorder since fifteen.
background.accessOpportunities: Regular therapy, medical follow-up, school workload adjustments, and family support.

timeline.story: In 2014, Zara liked dancing in the living room and making labels for household drawers. She changed the labels frequently, asking adults whether a different word would make it easier to find what they needed.

At six, she joined a children’s science club and particularly enjoyed experiments involving sound. During 2017, she also learned simple embroidery from an aunt, taking pride in choosing colors nobody else would have paired.

In 2018, Zara became absorbed in detective stories and wrote short mysteries with her brother. She enjoyed planting clues but often wrote endings in which the characters negotiated rather than identifying a single obvious villain.

During 2020, she stayed connected to friends through a shared drawing game and helped organize household meal plans. Some schoolwork felt repetitive, but she kept enjoying small experiments and long conversations with one close friend.

At twelve, she joined a school environmental group and helped map shade around the campus. By 2023, she was still active but increasingly bothered by the gap between the group’s ambitious posters and its limited practical follow-through.

In 2025, persistent low mood, fatigue, and loss of enjoyment led to a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Treatment and reduced commitments helped her return gradually to regular classes and occasional embroidery nights with her aunt.

At sixteen in 2026, Zara attends school consistently and is rebuilding activities cautiously. She is curious about a nearby Texas college’s summer workshop but wants a manageable trial, and she is uncertain which interests will feel meaningful as her energy improves.

avoids: Pressure to describe recovery as a straight line
ambitions: She imagines a steady adult routine with trusted people and enough energy left for personal projects.

biography.selfDescription: I am interested in things again, but I do not want to promise a giant new version of myself. Sometimes making one small thing with good colors is enough to remind me that I still have preferences.
openQuestions: Which former interests will return, change, or fall away?
How much activity supports recovery without exhausting her?

biography.name: Linh Cabrera

background.family: Lives with her adoptive parents and older adopted brother; both children have different birth-family contact arrangements that are discussed without comparison.
background.finances: Stable middle income from nursing and city employment; activity fees are manageable with planning.
background.geography: San Marcos, Texas, close to a river and a university campus.
background.cultureLanguages: Vietnamese American teenager in a Mexican American and white household; English predominates, with Spanish from relatives and beginner Vietnamese lessons by choice.
background.school: Public high school with outdoor education and art electives.
background.accessOpportunities: Has access to campus public events, river volunteers, and family-supported language tutoring.

timeline.story: Linh liked mixing paint and then trying to name the resulting colors. Her parents kept her sprawling pictures on a low wall, where she regularly changed their order to tell a new story.

She began weekend walks beside the river and asked why some banks had bare soil. A volunteer explained erosion using a handful of dirt, and Linh repeated the demonstration in the bathtub until cleanup rules were negotiated.

A school heritage project made her uncomfortable because classmates expected one simple family story. Her parents helped her present several relationships and unanswered questions, while letting her decide which private details belonged off the poster.

She learned to knit through video calls with an aunt during remote school. Counting stitches irritated her, but the repeated hand movement helped her listen to long conversations, and she made uneven but warmly received scarves.

Linh chose Vietnamese lessons after meeting another adopted teenager, then nearly quit when progress felt slow. Her teacher used songs and everyday phrases, making the lessons less like a test of whether she belonged.

River cleanups introduced her to collecting and classifying small debris. She created a collage from washed wrappers for art class, but resisted a teacher’s suggestion that every subsequent piece should carry an environmental message.

Now she combines outdoor volunteering, drawing, and occasional knitting while exploring university and community-college events nearby. She wants room to change her interests and her relationship to heritage without other people treating either as a solved assignment. A teacher’s enthusiastic interpretation of one drawing also taught her to say politely when an explanation did not match her intention.

avoids: Pressure to make every hobby meaningful
motivations: Freedom to revise her own story
ambitions: Imagines daily access to nature and a home where complicated family histories are ordinary.

biography.selfDescription: Sometimes a drawing is just colors I wanted to put together. I can care about the river and my family and where I came from without making every project explain all of it.
openQuestions: Will language lessons remain a personal choice over time?
Does she enjoy systematic field observation apart from volunteering?

questions.scene: A report argues that changes in one area affected travel in a neighboring area. Its readers need to understand the evidence, alternative explanations, and where the information is incomplete.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine explaining a fictional pattern using the sentence “This may be related to…, but we do not yet know…”. Identify evidence you would need to make the explanation stronger.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore communicating evidence-based relationships between places, including what the evidence cannot establish? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: A cautious sentence does not establish interest in developing and defending a full research explanation.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to communicate a research-based explanation of relationships between places, including the evidence and limits behind the geographic conclusions?

biography.name: Wyatt Sloane

background.family: Lives with parents and an older brother on a large property; family dinners are regular and disagreements tend to stay mild.
background.finances: Wealth from a family-owned distribution business; college tuition and travel are affordable.
background.geography: Outside Fredericksburg, Texas, with long drives to specialized activities.
background.cultureLanguages: White, English-speaking family with several generations in the Hill Country; church attendance is occasional.
background.school: Small private school; good classroom support but few electives and a fairly uniform peer group.
background.accessOpportunities: Has abundant material resources but low exposure to unfamiliar work, communities, or independent responsibility.

timeline.story: Wyatt liked following the groundskeeper as he checked irrigation and collected fallen branches. He asked many questions but preferred inventing stories about the broken branches to helping carry an entire load to the trailer.

His parents tried horseback riding lessons and tennis. He enjoyed being outdoors but disliked correction in front of other children, so both activities ended before he had enough practice to feel competent or decide much else.

He received a sophisticated building set and completed several models by following instructions. When asked to design something original, he became frustrated and put the pieces away, unsure how to begin without knowing the finished shape.

Remote school left him with plenty of space and few nearby peers. He watched cooking videos but rarely used the kitchen until his brother challenged him to make a complete breakfast without asking adults for each next step.

He began baking biscuits on Sundays and liked repeating a familiar recipe. A teacher encouraged him to document variations; Wyatt resisted at first, then became interested when a slightly different method actually changed the texture.

A family trip included a crowded city market that made him both uncomfortable and curious. He later asked to join a school service outing and enjoyed sorting supplies, while realizing he had never before followed a bus timetable.

He now bakes, plays casual online games, and helps with routine supply sorting several times a semester. College is assumed at home, but he cannot yet name what he wants from it besides friendships and a chance to become less dependent on familiar arrangements.

avoids: Open-ended tasks without an entry point
ambitions: Imagines a comfortable home but wants to learn how to run its ordinary routines himself.

biography.selfDescription: I know a lot of things are available to me, but available isn't the same as familiar. I'd like to get better at trying something before I decide that feeling awkward means I don't like it.
openQuestions: Would a less familiar environment broaden choices or initially reinforce avoidance?
Does repetition appeal independently of having a clear recipe?

questions.scene: A research team compares plant material from several locations. Each sample must be collected and prepared consistently so a mix-up or difference in handling does not distort the study.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Without collecting anything, imagine three fictional plant samples from different locations. Decide what labels and preparation notes would help a team compare them fairly.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore carefully collecting and preparing biological samples to support the study of living things? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Liking plants or animals does not establish interest in repeated sample preparation and handling procedures.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to collect and prepare biological samples, such as plants, water, or animal material, to help scientists study living things?

questions.scene: A study compares how seeds develop under two defined conditions. Following the procedure, observing consistently, and recording unexpected results matter as much as the hoped-for outcome.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: In your head, plan a fictional record for two groups of seeds. Name one thing to keep the same, one observation to record, and how to note a result that surprises you; do not run an experiment.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore carrying out biological experiments carefully and recording observations for a research team? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: This imagined record does not test experimental skills or establish interest in the repetition of research procedures.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to carry out biological experiments carefully, observe what happens, and record results for a research team?

biography.name: Jonas Loke

background.family: Lives with his parents and two sisters; an aunt and cousins in Beaumont host occasional visits and maintain frequent video calls.
background.finances: Modest stable income from a small delivery business and school cafeteria work.
background.geography: A small town outside Salem, Oregon.
background.cultureLanguages: Marshallese American family using Marshallese and English; household members differ in how much community activity they want each week.
background.school: Public high school with agricultural science, choir, and a regional vocational partnership.
background.accessOpportunities: Local community college events are easiest; Lamar-area public programs during Texas family visits are plausible, with nonresident costs and distance unresolved.

timeline.story: Jonas liked helping load empty boxes into the family van and asking which house came next. At home he planted seeds from fruit and was surprised that most did not sprout.
A school garden gave him a more reliable way to grow things. He enjoyed measuring leaves and disliked the competitive classroom chart that treated the tallest plant as the best.

He joined a children's choir and discovered he liked singing with others more than speaking alone. A cousin taught him simple video editing, but he preferred recording plant growth to making fast entertaining clips.

Jonas helped his parents plan a delivery route and enjoyed the practical geography. Customers' small talk felt awkward until he learned a few opening questions. He also began making tiny paper sculptures while listening to music.

A vocational workshop introduced welding, which relatives expected him to enjoy. He liked the precision but not the heat and protective clothing. He chose a horticulture elective afterward, without deciding whether that meant anything about future study.

He visited cousins in Beaumont and toured a community garden and public campus event. Humid-weather plants fascinated him. Back home he helped younger students compare growing conditions and learned to stop correcting every imperfect measurement immediately.

Jonas sings in choir, works in the school greenhouse, and occasionally rides delivery routes with a parent. He is considering a longer Texas visit but does not know whether the appeal is family, unfamiliar plants, or the idea of a different landscape.

avoids: Treating growth as a simple competition
motivations: Understanding why living things respond differently
Maintaining family connections without copying every family interest
ambitions: Compare the same plant in two climates
He imagines an adult home with room to grow plants and sing with other people, though he is unsure how far from family to live
struggles: Quiet participation can hide how much he knows

biography.selfDescription: I do not mind repeating an observation if something living keeps changing. I like a group sound better than a solo, but I still want people to notice my part.
openQuestions: Would he enjoy horticultural work when it includes routine commercial demands?
What would a longer stay away reveal about his preferred distance from family?

biography.name: Miles Bennett

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger sister; nearby grandparents visit often.
background.geography: A quiet neighborhood in Round Rock, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking household with familiar family holiday traditions and no strong religious involvement.
background.school: Public high school with accessible teachers and several laboratory classes.
background.accessOpportunities: Reliable computer, rides, occasional tutoring, clubs, and ordinary family vacations.

timeline.story: Miles liked building short ramps for toy cars but usually asked an adult to fix them when the cars fell off. He also watched cartoons and played restaurant with his sister. His parents remember an easygoing child who sometimes abandoned a game as soon as somebody changed the rules.

He enjoyed a classroom experiment using magnets and asked for a kit afterward. Most pieces ended up mixed with other toys. He liked having his grandfather demonstrate things one step at a time, but did not spontaneously write observations or develop projects beyond the instructions provided.

Miles spent more time swimming and trading game cards than doing science activities. A broken flashlight interested him for one afternoon, although his mother completed the repair. He was embarrassed when classmates finished multiplication faster and needed reassurance before agreeing to practice where anyone could hear him.

At home during remote school, he watched videos about motion and paused them to copy diagrams. The mathematics often escaped him. He asked his father questions, got irritated when the answer seemed too quick, and returned later. He also ignored several assignments whose instructions he understood perfectly well.

An introductory physics unit interested him enough to attempt optional problems. His first answers were mostly wrong. A teacher showed him how to draw the situation before choosing an equation, and he began using that routine. He liked the small improvement but still needed help recognizing which quantities mattered.

Miles chose a demanding physical science class with his parents’ support. He attended extra help repeatedly and sometimes took twice as long as friends on homework. He enjoyed tracing where his reasoning failed. He disliked the report formatting and occasionally let a classmate do too much of the shared writing.

He voluntarily continues with physics even after an uneven examination result. He asks for hints, tries another approach, and sometimes needs someone to work the entire example beside him. He likes the effort when it makes a confusing idea clearer, but cannot yet tell whether he would enjoy prolonged independent work.

enjoys: Understanding motion problems after several attempts
Comparing an experiment with his prediction
activities: Works through practice examples with a tutor
Plays games with friends most weekends
demonstratedSkills: Returns to difficult questions after frustration
Asks specific questions about a mistaken step
motivations: Enjoys the moment a difficult explanation makes sense
Wants to see what practice can change
ambitions: Solve a whole unfamiliar problem without a hint eventually
struggles: Can depend too much on a partner for writing
Sometimes mistakes familiarity with an example for understanding
practicalConstraints: Homework takes time from other activities
Needs to schedule help before class deadlines

biography.selfDescription: I am the person still doing problem two when my friend finishes the page. I actually want to keep doing it most days. I do not know if that counts as being good at it, and I get annoyed when people act like trying makes it easy.
openQuestions: How will interest hold up when support is less immediate?
Does he enjoy experimental work as much as worked problems?
Which writing responsibilities will he take independently?

questions.scene: A team can observe a distant object only at certain times and with limited precision. Its investigation and report must make the question, evidence, uncertainty, and observation limits clear.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine a fictional object was observed on only three nights. Consider a question the observations might address and a claim you would avoid making without more data.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore designing and communicating a defensible investigation of a question about space, including uncertainty? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Naming a limitation does not establish interest in planning and defending a full astronomical investigation.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to design and communicate a defensible investigation of an astronomical question, including uncertainty and the limits of available observations?

questions.scene: A physical investigation’s result depends on assumptions and measurements with uncertainty. Other people need enough detail to examine the reasoning and, where possible, repeat the investigation.
questions.tryIt: Optional, up to two minutes: Imagine describing a fictional measurement to someone who was absent. Think of an assumption, a measurement detail, and an uncertainty they would need before trying to reproduce the result.
questions.reflection: Would you want to explore reporting physical research clearly enough for others to examine its assumptions and repeat its methods? It is equally okay to choose no, unsure, or unfamiliar.
questions.limit: Listing three details does not establish interest in the full discipline of documenting and defending research.
questions.underlyingInterest: Would you like to learn to report physical research with enough detail about assumptions and uncertainty for others to examine or repeat the investigation?
